Author: @redwoodxrings
Content:
It might  be the case that the government pretends to declassify material on old projects they've described as being failures, that the project did not provide enough useful results to be considered worthwhile or affordable enough to continue. All the  projects described in this video would fall under this category. When people read material that appears to be a declassified file about an old CIA project about using cats as spies many years ago, if someone in our modern day noticed how their cat kept jumping on his lap, craving affection every time he and his hitman brother discussed their plans to take out some politician running for a position, it's highly probable that if the brother said anything to the hitman brother about wondering whether the cat was somehow being used as a spy, and possibly able to transmit the audio from their conversations, that the hitman brother could say something like, "Bro, don't you know they already tried turning cats into spies years ago?... Yeah, before we were even born they implanted all this spy equipment in cats, but it didn't work, because the cats would stay put, and one of them got ran over, so they squashed the whole project. Yeah, man, it doesn't work. They learned that years ago." 

So, if we are led to believe that  the government "already did that, and it doesn't work", then we will be dismissive, not suspicious of the ways that these animals might actually be used as spies in our modern day. Declassifying material that describes an old project ended years ago - successful or not - leaves us under the impression there's no way they're doing the same thing, today. 

MKUltra was supposedly leaked. They allegedly burned almost all of the paperwork that spanned research conducted on American citizens for decades, and they left behind a small portion of this material, available today. We are told CIA ended MKUltra after determining it was unable to deliver any(more?) useful results. So, we are left to assume the government training and using psychic spies, and other things that were part of MKUltra is a thing of the past, and therefore, not something we have continued and advanced even further to be used in modern day. If we are unaware of something's existence, then we will be oblivious to its presence and use in modern day if indeed, the government has continued to develop the project.  

From using animals as spies, to developing a truth serum, these declassified documents convince us that these things don't exist today, when they very well could, and in my opinion, probably do. These declassified documents would leave people thinking that I am a delusional and paranoid person for believing that my dog was used as a type of optical spy. What if the acoustikitty - if it really was run over - left researchers deciding they needed to use dogs, instead, since dogs will be responsive to audible commands. Maybe they abandoned that project with cats, but then created a new project using dogs, which were able to hear a faint voice only they could hear, which allowed the researchers to train the dogs to sit or lay down in the desired position for as long as necessary. I wouldn't be the least bit surprised to learn the government has even more advanced versions of each one of these projects described in this video, and that not all documents are declassified because of FOIA requests, but deliberately released by the related agency during a time the same agency is currently engaged in a modernized version of the same project. By redacting some information, and maybe editing conclusions to state a successful project was considered a failure (I know it's highly controversial and accusatory to speculate the government might  be doctoring the documents released to the public, but from a defense perspective, it is a good idea to mislead our adversaries instead of teaching them everything that we've found success in, because influencing adversaries to not spend time or money researching or and/or developing something America has deemed useless is, in itself, a type of defense strategy. And the same can be true for the opposite conditions: by convincing adversaries we have had success with things that were failures can cause our adversaries to spend vast amounts of time and money on projects that will likely never bring them success in the way they'd been led to believe American had.)

We don't like being lied to, but it is often in our best interest, from a defense perspective. And for that reason, I believe that many of these projects were actually successful, and that we have developed even more advanced versions of things we've been led to believe were abandoned as ideas decades ago.

Author: @kittycatcitycat
Content: Raven psychology is interesting.  When several ravens remained aggressive to Duda over time, even though they knew his routine and knew he posed no threat and that fighting him offered no great reward, we really can ask why and think of interesting answers.  Were they bored enough to do this just for entertainment, the way smart animals like puzzles?  Did they think he was running surveillance on THEIR space and would eventually move in on their nests, or valuable resources to them?  I've never heard seagulls praised for their brain power, so I tend to assume they'd just be protecting nesting areas and maybe it's as simple as that with these ravens too.  Still, smart animals with strange human-assigned goals fighting repeatedly with animals of their own kind is a unique situation to think about animal thought process of all the creatures involved.  And seagulls sure are successful, so it would be worth it to know how they think, and why their thinking doesn't typically get the hype that raven, crow or pigeon thinking does.  Certainly their brain work for THEM.

Author: @DixonCyderBusch
Content:
Homing pigeons possess a truly remarkable ability to find their way home, even from unfamiliar locations many miles away. While the exact mechanisms are still a subject of ongoing scientific research, it's generally accepted that they use a combination of sophisticated navigation tools:
1. Sun Compass:
 * Pigeons, like many birds, can use the sun's position in the sky to determine direction. They account for the sun's movement throughout the day, essentially having an internal clock that allows them to adjust their bearing.
2. Earth's Magnetic Field (Magnetoreception):
 * This is a significant factor. Pigeons appear to be able to detect and use the Earth's magnetic field as a compass. While early theories suggested iron particles in their beaks were responsible, more recent research points to cells in their inner ear or even light-sensitive proteins in their eyes (cryptochromes) that allow them to "see" magnetic fields. This "magnetic sense" can provide a sense of direction and even help them determine their location relative to home.
3. Olfactory Navigation (Sense of Smell):
 * This is a powerful and well-supported theory. Pigeons seem to create "olfactory maps" of their environment. They can detect subtle variations in atmospheric odors and chemical compounds that are unique to different locations. By smelling the air, they can essentially create a "scent map" that helps them navigate back to their home loft, especially over unfamiliar terrain.
4. Infrasound:
 * Some research suggests pigeons may also use low-frequency sound waves (infrasound) that are inaudible to humans. These sounds are generated by natural phenomena like ocean waves and geographical features, and they could provide a unique acoustic "signature" for different areas, guiding the pigeons home.
5. Visual Landmarks:
 * Once pigeons get closer to home, or when they're navigating familiar routes, they rely heavily on visual landmarks. They memorize prominent features like rivers, roads, buildings, and even mountain ranges to guide them. Over time, they can learn highly efficient, stereotyped flight paths.
"Map and Compass" Model:
Many researchers believe that pigeon navigation is best explained by a "map and compass" model.
 * Compass mechanism: This is likely attributed to the sun and/or magnetic field, allowing them to orient themselves in a particular direction.
 * Map mechanism: This is more complex and highly debated, but likely involves olfaction and potentially infrasound, allowing them to determine their position relative to their home loft.
It's important to note that pigeons don't just inherently "know" where their home is from anywhere. Homing pigeons are often trained by gradually increasing the distance they are released from their loft. This training helps them develop and refine their navigational skills, building their "map" and strengthening their ability to use these diverse cues in combination.
